description:
Our goal in this hackathon is to push limits in tech, solve real problems, and prove that age doesn't define output — even high school students can engineer high-impact products.
We’re building a web strategy game where players design and manage space missions — balancing mass, budget, power, and science goals within a realistic 48-hour scope.
Looking for:
• Web Game Developers
• Graphic Designers
• Math, Physics, or Space Enthusiasts
summary:
Star Chasers is a free browser game for kids aged 9–15, in Russian and English, built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players design a mission the way NASA does. They pick a launch day in Mission Control, build a rocket from parts, fly it themselves, and then explore the Moon or Mars to collect samples.

Every step uses real science instead of cartoon rules. The flight follows real physics: thrust, drag, gravity and the rocket equation. Mission Control shows today's Moon phase, launch-site weather from NASA POWER checked against simplified launch rules, Mars launch windows, the Δv budget and a mission grant the rocket must fit. Players can relive Artemis II on its real April 2026 launch days. In the sample lab, they identify rocks the way Perseverance's SuperCam and WATSON instruments do: reading element lines in a laser spectrum and textures under a close-up camera.

Failure is explained in plain words, for example "you are 400 m/s short: add a tank". Players learn by trying again rather than by memorising. The game runs on any phone or laptop with no install and no account.
details:
What it does
Star Chasers is a browser game that walks a player through a whole space mission, one step at a time.
Mission Control. Pick a launch day from the next 14. Each day shows the Moon's phase and distance, measured launch-site weather from NASA POWER, and a GO / NO GO verdict based on simplified launch rules (wind, storms, cloud, cold). It also shows how long the trip will take, whether the landing site will be in daylight on arrival, Mars launch windows, the Δv budget and the rocket's cost against the mission grant. A "Relive Artemis II" mode loads the real launch days of April 2026, with the weather NASA measured on them. A NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day panel is translated into Russian.
Builder. Drag engines, tanks, fins, separators and parachutes onto a stack and watch mass, Δv, thrust-to-weight ratio and stability update live. Hovering over a part opens a plate with its numbers, the physics formula it obeys and a real NASA part for comparison (RS-25, F-1, RL10, Orion's parachutes).
Flight. The player pilots the rocket in a 2D physics simulation with gravity, drag that changes with air density, thrust that changes with air pressure, staging, a parachute, and the wind of the chosen launch day.
Exploration. Walk or drive a rover on the Moon or Mars, drill samples to complete a task list, and beam the data home.
Sample lab. Identify the samples the way Perseverance's SuperCam and WATSON instruments do. Match element lines in a laser spectrum, focus a close-up camera, and read the rock's texture to tell whether it formed from lava, water, ice or an impact. A guided tutorial comes first, then a timed challenge.
Benefits and intended impact
Kids learn spaceflight by doing it, not by reading about it. The result depends only on the player's own design and choices. When a mission fails, the game explains why in plain words, for example "you ran out of fuel at 4.2 km: add a tank". Real data shows that space missions depend on weather, the Moon's position, physics and money all at once. The game runs on any phone, tablet or laptop with no install, no account and no server, and it works in Russian and English. That makes it easy to use in schools, including classrooms with weak hardware.
Tools and technology
Code: TypeScript, Phaser 3 (game engine), Vite (build), Vitest (124 unit tests covering physics, the Moon ephemeris, launch rules and lab data).
Data: NASA POWER API (launch-site weather), NASA APOD API (picture of the day), MyMemory API (translation into Russian).
Science: Moon and Sun positions computed with Jean Meeus's formulas (checked against the March 2026 lunar eclipse), JPL planet positions, vis-viva and Kepler's equation for trip times, Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation.
Hosting: GitHub Pages, deployed automatically with GitHub Actions.
Art and media: AI image and video tools (Grok for game art, Higgsfield Seedance 2.5 for the intro trailer), plus an AI coding assistant.
Creativity
The game links four parts that are usually separate: mission planning, rocket engineering, piloting and lab science. A choice made in one part carries into the next. A lighter rocket arrives sooner, a windy launch day pushes the rocket sideways, and an over-budget design can't launch. Real NASA instruments are turned into puzzles kids can solve, and players can re-fly a real mission, Artemis II, on its actual launch days.
Factors we considered
Accuracy vs fun: the world is scaled to 1/10 size so flights take minutes, but real formulas drive everything, and the real-world numbers are shown next to the game numbers.
Accessibility: big buttons, separate touch and keyboard controls, full Russian and English, a "rotate your device" screen and fullscreen on phones.
Reliability: every live data source has a cache and an offline fallback, so the game never stops working without internet.
Honesty with data: NASA POWER has no forecasts, so the game uses past years' weather for future days and says so on screen.
